title: Quality Management -- Definition/Introduction
content: Quality in the traditional sense pertains to whether a product or service meets its expected characteristics and satisfies the consumer—in other words, how well it does what it is meant to do. [1] For healthcare, the Institute of Medicine (IOM) has defined quality as “the degree to which health care services for individuals and populations increase the likelihood of desired outcomes and are consistent with current professional knowledge.” [2]

title: Quality Management -- Definition/Introduction -- Healthcare Quality Domains
content: The goal of the healthcare system is to provide ideal care from a qualified provider in an appropriate setting for a particular patient. In other words, the patient is to receive the best possible care (ie, standard of care based on evidence-based medicine) by a provider with the right expertise in a setting that maximizes efficiency and minimizes risk and abuse of resources—all the while treating the patient with respect and allowing involvement in the care plan as the patient desires. In recent years, the IOM identified 6 domains that help achieve a high degree of quality: health care must be safe, effective, patient-centered, timely, efficient, and equitable. [3] Meeting all these domains is at the core of quality management. “Safe” pertains to preventing harm to patients stemming from the care they are receiving. “Effective” uses evidence-based care and appropriately utilizes resources. “Patient-centered” refers to care that is responsive and considerate of the patient’s inclinations, needs, and values, guiding all clinical decisions. “Timely” focuses on preventing delays in care. Efficiency relates to minimizing or avoiding waste of resources such as supplies and time. Lastly, “equitable” indicates providing care to all patients regardless of characteristics such as appearance, socioeconomic status, and values. The success of health care in achieving these quality domains can be measured by collecting data and evaluating “the 5 D’s:”  death (mortality), disability (morbidity), disease (resolution or persistence of disease following treatment), discomfort (the process of providing medical care) and dissatisfaction (the patient’s experience during the process of providing care). [4]

title: Quality Management -- Definition/Introduction -- Quality Management
content: In healthcare, quality management refers to the administration of systems design, policies, and processes that minimize, if not eliminate, harm while optimizing patient care and outcomes. [5] The objective of quality management is to ensure that a product, service, or organization consistently fulfills its intended purpose. To achieve this, data is continuously collected, and the process is continually refined to create an optimal product or service that fulfills its intended purpose and satisfies the consumer. Further data is then collected to ensure that no additional changes are necessary. Quality management systems are tools used to implement quality management and to organize, standardize, and improve activities involving products or services aimed at customers. [5] [6] By measuring outcomes and effects of different factors via data collection, issues within the system are identified, and evidence-based medicine and resources are used to develop or alter processes to improve the quality of care. Information is then collected on new outcomes to determine whether the changes were beneficial or whether other alterations are required. The ultimate goal is to achieve consistent, high-level care with minimal morbidity, mortality, disease, discomfort, and to ensure high patient satisfaction while meeting or exceeding all 6 IOM domains (safe, effective, patient-centered, timely, efficient, and equitable care).

title: Quality Management -- Definition/Introduction -- Quality Management
content: Here is the definition of quality and quality management as applied to a case scenario, noting that all 6 IOM domains are easily identifiable. A trauma hospital offers a service: to safely and efficiently assess and stabilize a patient after suffering a traumatic injury. Regardless of the patient’s history or background, the patient is seen within a specific time frame based on the trauma's acuity. To achieve optimal care, all trauma providers are all trained in Advanced Trauma Life Support to keep the evaluation of this patient organized and address the most life-threatening injuries first. [7] Despite the intensity of a trauma scenario, all efforts need to respect a patient’s privacy and goals of care. After the patient’s hospital stay, quality management teams measure data, including adverse events, patient outcomes, and experience (ie, the 5 D’s) to optimize future care and make changes and recommendations as needed.

title: Quality Management -- Issues of Concern -- Quality Management Models and Approaches
content: There are different Quality Management models and approaches. A recent review of existing quality management models for inpatient healthcare identified 64 different models, 17 of which gained recognition as significant to current healthcare practice. [8] Below, we discuss a few of the models and potential issues.

title: Quality Management -- Issues of Concern -- Total quality management
content: Total quality management (TQM) is an “integrated process involving all systems and employees in a continuous effort to improve quality, reduce cost, and enhance service to the customer.” [9] To identify the essential elements of TQM in healthcare, researchers conducted a meta-analysis to determine the crucial factors for its success. Among these were leadership, employee involvement, training, process management, support from upper administration, and planning. [10] Interestingly, another meta-analysis identified factors contributing to the failure of TQM implementation in healthcare. [11] These include a lack of employee involvement (specifically by physicians), inconsistent upper-management support, poor leadership, a lack of a quality-oriented culture, insufficient education and training, and inadequate resources. [11] The similarity between the 2 studies indicates the essential elements of a healthcare organization. The development of these features leads to success, but inadequacies result in the breakdown of TQM implementation.

title: Quality Management -- Issues of Concern -- Continuous quality improvement
content: Continuous quality improvement (CQI) involves systematically using tools and processes to identify and analyze strengths and barriers within an organization, and to continually test and improve outcomes. CQI methods originated in business and engineering fields post-World War II and have been used in healthcare over the last few decades. [12] In healthcare, CQI’s approach to improvement connects the most recent best evidence with current practices to achieve better patient outcomes. [13] While finding success in different aspects of healthcare, some areas have identified barriers with CQI. [14] For example, the implementation of CQI programs in colonoscopy services identified a significant knowledge gap regarding barriers and facilitators among nurses, patients, and managers. [14]

title: Quality Management -- Issues of Concern -- Joint Commission on Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations
content: Accreditation of healthcare organizations has been another Quality Management pathway. An example is The Joint Commission, which is a voluntary process that enforces, monitors, and improves upon the quality of healthcare in the United States and internationally. [15] [16] It currently evaluates more than 20,000 healthcare organizations and is the largest accreditation group in the nation. The Joint Commission assesses whether a facility meets accreditation standards for healthcare quality, including incorporating programs that perform quality measurement, evaluation, and improvement of patient outcomes. Accreditation also provides external validity to hospital administration and increases transparency to patients and providers. title: Quality Management -- Issues of Concern -- Joint Commission on Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations
content: The question lingers: what is accreditation, and why is it important for hospitals? When a hospital is accredited, its performance is within the range of nationally accepted criteria based on government guidelines; this means the hospital has a system of assessment and self-improvement, resulting in compliance with the standard of care and, ideally, better outcomes. Additionally, an accredited hospital enhances public confidence (ie, satisfies consumers).

title: Quality Management -- Issues of Concern -- Joint Commission on Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations
content: A recent study examined whether patients admitted to accredited US hospitals have better outcomes and whether accreditation by The Joint Commission provides additional benefits for patients compared with other independent accrediting organizations. [18] Results indicated that US hospitals accredited by independent organizations did not experience significantly lower mortality but did demonstrate slightly lower readmission rates for the 15 most common medical conditions. Also, there was no indication that patients choosing a hospital accredited by The Joint Commission had any healthcare benefits compared to a hospital accredited by another independent accrediting organization. Of note, the study had limitations due to its observational design.

title: Quality Management -- Clinical Significance -- Principles of Quality Management
content: In the field of quality management, the International Organization for Standardization identified 7 basic principles that, when properly applied, can aid in evaluating and optimizing a service or product through data collection, process improvement, and coordination among involved parties. [5] The International Organization for Standardization is an independent international group of voluntary experts that develops consensus-based and market-relevant International Standards. These quality management principles, or QMPs, include customer focus, leadership, people engagement, process approach, improvement, evidence-based decision-making, and relationship management. [5]

title: Quality Management -- Clinical Significance -- Principles of Quality Management
content: Customer service/ customer satisfaction is essential to quality management. Without customers, there is no one to offer a service or product. The goal is to keep customers returning by meeting their expectations and building confidence in the offered product or service. While an institution’s employees are each other’s customers, the ultimate customer is the patient. Both patient experience and patient outcomes define healthcare quality. While we do not want patients cycling through the hospital more than necessary, the hospital would like to be their provider of choice if hospitalization is warranted.  By taking into account the patient’s perception of care—did they feel respected, were they included in the plan of care—and by fulfilling patient expectations, the financial aspect of the healthcare system also thrives. For example, patients who come to the emergency department expect to be seen and cared for in a timely fashion. One way to ensure a timely evaluation is to record when each team member arrives to evaluate a patient.  As mentioned, while the patient remains the ultimate customer of healthcare institutions, it should also be emphasized that people at every level of the organization are one another’s customers, and their performance is intertwined. The goal is for each group/department to meet or exceed the needs and expectations of the groups or departments they serve. This approach allows the entire institution to deliver the utmost care and safety to its patients. For example, the paramedics rely on the emergency department to be ready for a patient, and, in turn, the emergency physician relies on quick test results from the laboratory and radiology departments.

title: Quality Management -- Clinical Significance -- Principles of Quality Management
content: Leadership is necessary at all levels to reinforce the goals and purpose of an organization, product, or service. Leadership at the top is needed to set the organization's mission and vision and to promote support, efficiency, and open communication by encouraging a unified, attainable approach to achieving objectives through predefined processes/policies. Returning to our trauma scenario, the trauma surgeon ensures that the Advanced Trauma Life Support protocol is followed and appropriate interventions are taken, whether it be a chest tube insertion or exploratory surgery. Their job is to encourage the team and communicate the patient's needs to those in the trauma bay and to other involved parties, such as the operating room or interventional radiology.

title: Quality Management -- Clinical Significance -- Principles of Quality Management
content: Engagement of people at all levels is essential to achieving the objectives of an organization, product, or service. Healthcare institutions are built on the strength and commitment of its people. It is ideal to have enthusiastic workers who are competent in their particular role within the process. By respecting people at all levels, job satisfaction, motivation, and collaboration improve; thus, there is better feedback for improvement across all stages of the process. For example, in the operating room, all providers have a known, pre-identified role, whether it is the scrub technician monitoring the sterile field, the anesthesiologist evaluating patient vitals, or the operating room nurse leading the pre-operative timeout. Feedback from all providers is essential to ensure they can perform their job at the highest level possible.

title: Quality Management -- Clinical Significance -- Principles of Quality Management
content: The process approach is the key to achieving a consistent, desired outcome. While it is often multiple interrelated processes that are required to achieve the ideal outcome, all of them must function consistently and as a unit to thrive. Once standardized, individual processes require continuous assessment and appropriate optimization if areas needing improvement are identified. For a cardiac arrest patient, the process begins the moment 9-1-1 is called and continues through EMS assessment, handoff to the emergency department team, performance of advanced cardiac life support protocols, and throughout the patient’s hospital stay. While each aspect of care provides different services, each must be standardized and eventually optimized to achieve the ultimate objective of getting the patient home safely with minimal morbidity.

title: Quality Management -- Clinical Significance -- Principles of Quality Management
content: Improvement is the key to success. By continually collecting data and assessing outcomes, opportunities for improvement come to light and can be addressed. The end result is better quality through improved performance, outcomes, and customer satisfaction. Root cause analysis and failure mode and effects analysis are 2 methods used to examine sentinel events and promote improvement within a health care system. In the medical world, there are frequent morbidity and mortality conferences and peer review sessions regarding patients who do not have ideal outcomes. What could have been done better throughout all stages of care? Was the patient seen and evaluated in a timely fashion? Was there a missed diagnosis? Were the appropriate interventions implemented based on the clinical picture? Was there a breach in the standard of care? What can possibly remedy this?

title: Quality Management -- Clinical Significance -- Principles of Quality Management
content: Evidence-based decision-making (ie, evidence-based medicine) is the evaluation of facts, evidence, cause-and-effect relationships, and other data to deliver the best product or service. By basing decisions on facts, processes can be standardized, thereby increasing the likelihood of consistent, desired results. After changing processes, it is important to continue monitoring outcomes to determine whether corrective actions are achieving the desired endpoint. By repeating this cycle and sharing results with other health care institutions, quality care and ideal outcomes can be widely replicated.  For example, Level 1 trauma centers have in-house trauma and neurosurgeons available around the clock to ensure expedited care, because studies and clinical experience have shown that immediate access to these physicians reduces costs, time to intervention, and hospital length of stay. [19]

title: Quality Management -- Clinical Significance -- Principles of Quality Management
content: Relationship management is essential for an organization to thrive. Supportive relationships with suppliers, retailers, monetary providers, and partners must be maintained, as well as a common understanding of goals across all parties. Shared goals and understanding also ensure a reliable supply chain, enabling the institution to deliver high-quality care to its patients consistently. For example, donations to a hospital allow a new interventional radiology suite to be built with the latest technology, enabling patients to be seen more quickly and providers to have more space and resources for treatment.

title: Quality Management -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Interventions
content: Pioneers such as Ignaz Semmelweis and Florence Nightingale were among the first in medicine to implement process changes based on observation and data collection. [20] [21] Semmelweis was a Hungarian physician who observed higher mortality among obstetric patients cared for by physicians than by nurse-midwives at the same institution. It was not until one of his colleagues suffered an injury and death due to a scalpel puncture while performing an autopsy that Semmelweis noted an association. He instituted a policy of handwashing after completing autopsies and prior to delivering babies, and, as a result, the mortality rate decreased substantially to a level similar to that of midwives. As for Florence Nightingale, an English nurse, she is known for her observation of poor healthcare conditions while serving the British army. She was also an advocate for the development of standardized, formal nursing education and was recognized as one of the earlier adopters of evidence-based medicine using data and data visualization. [21]

title: Quality Management -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Interventions
content: Going forward, healthcare education should incorporate quality management into its curriculum and interprofessional collaboration efforts. By introducing medical, healthcare, and allied professions students and practitioners to quality improvement, they are more likely to reap the benefits of improved patient outcomes and satisfaction. Not to mention, knowledge of the benefits of quality management enhances compliance and feedback across all areas of the health care system. With insurance companies denying reimbursement for issues such as foley catheter- or central line-associated infections acquired during a hospital stay, the push for quality improvement intensifies. More than just meeting criteria for reimbursement, quality management, when used to its full potential, encourages optimal outcomes, supreme patient satisfaction, reduces work by improving efficiency, and lowers overall patient and hospital costs. It all begins with collecting data to identify problems, evaluating possible causes, determining potential solutions, and subsequently monitoring corrective actions for effectiveness. These measures not only improve patient outcomes, experience, and hospital performance, but also fulfill requirements set by the Joint Commission and insurance companies. Whether it is participating in a trauma morbidity and mortality conference, conducting a root-cause analysis after a sentinel event, or assessing rates of catheter-associated UTI, the importance of quality improvement cannot be overemphasized. They should continue to grow as a part of conventional health care education and practice.
